newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Spacecraft readied for stricken Mir's relief crew.
newsitem.headline: Spacecraft readied for stricken Mir's relief crew.

text.p: A spacecraft which will take a relief crew to Russia's stricken Mir space station was placed on a launch pad on Sunday at the Baikonur cosmodrome in preparation for Tuesday's launch.
A worker in grubby white overalls wiped down part of the Soyuz-U rocket booster before it was rolled out of a hangar along a railway track to the launch pad.

A hoist pushed the rocket, with a Soyuz TM-26 spacecraft on top, into vertical position under a glaring sun at the launch site in the middle of parched steppe land in neighbouring Kazakhstan, where Baikonur is located.
Russian cosmonauts Anatoly Solovyov and Pavel Vinogradov will blast off to Mir aboard the Soyuz on Tuesday to relieve the crippled space station's tired and accident-prone crew.
They will carry out the risky repairs needed to restore full power to Mir later this month.
A resupply ship crashed into Mir on June 25 damaging solar panels which provide part of the 11-year-old space station's power.
NASA physicist Michael Foale will stay on board until a U.S. shuttle arrives in September, when he will be replaced by U.S. astronaut David Wolf.
On August 20, the cosmonauts will don spacesuits to try to reattach interior cables to the solar panels outside Mir's punctured Spektr module.
The cosmonauts, who are expected to stay in orbit for about six months, will later make their first spacewalk to inspect the hole in the module.
